Since 1942, the clock tower of Notre Dame de l’Assomption has chimed an 8th-century hymn every 15 minutes … day and night. Between 10pm and 7am, the bells ring 37 times, adding up to more than 700 individual chimes. Continue reading...

articles.author: George Francis Lee
articles.content: From Helsinki to Istanbul, independent developers are putting Grand Theft Auto-style action on their home streets, and without billion-dollar budgets. They tell us how they do it Like most kids who shouldn’t have been playing Grand Theft Auto III in 2001, Eamonn Swayah imagined a version of Rockstar Games’ groundbreaking criminal sandbox set in his own back yard. In his case, that was a Manchester council estate, complete with local accents, driving on the left, and plenty of ways to hustle. He didn’t know it, but swapping the game’s facsimile of early 2000s New York City for a different setting was an idea he shared with many watchful game developers. Rockstar’s 3D open world template, it turned out, could be plonked in just about any location, so long as it had people and enough cars to run them over with. After GTA III attracted immense commercial success (and controversy), dozens of copycats and spiritual sequels hit the market throughout the 00s and 2010s. Gamers had a pithy name for them: “GTA clones”. Continue reading...

articles.author: Stuart Heritage
articles.content: Fast becoming an essential Christmas tradition, the Sherlock creator’s latest in this classic horror series – starring Martin Freeman, effectively playing Charles Dickens – is inventive, joyous and, at times, genuinely terrifying For all the doom and gloom about the death of Christmas television as a collective event – nice try bunging on a normal Friday schedule with the word “Christmas” in front of each show, ITV, but we see you – can we at least agree that the most unsung festive TV tradition is Mark Gatiss’s continued revival of A Ghost Story for Christmas? For years now, it has functioned as a dark mirror to the Julia Donaldson animations. Each new episode is small and self-contained, clearly made on a shoestring but containing at least one moment of bone-deep foundational horror. And, as much as this might make the purists clutch their pearls, I would argue that the Gatiss run – starting in earnest in 2018 after a 2013 one-off, with a fallow year for Covid – deserves to be seen as the pinnacle of the series. True, the 1970s version contained classics including The Signalman and A Warning to the Curious, but only eight of those were made. The Bride’s Chamber is Gatiss’s ninth. Continue reading...

articles.author: Sarah Wynn-Williams
articles.content: Since writing her bestselling exposé, the former employee has been forbidden from speaking publicly about Meta. In an exclusive extract from her Orwell lecture, she describes life under a gag order – and why it’s time to speak out against big tech In 2011, Sarah Wynn-Williams was appointed director of global public policy at Facebook (now Meta). Over seven years, she brokered meetings with world leaders and contributed to public policy strategy in developing nations across three continents . She left the company in 2017 and in March 2025 published a book about her time at Meta. Careless People: A Story of Where I Used to Work describes a journey of disillusionment with a company that she was sure would change the world for the better to one “helping some of the worst people in the world do terrible things ”. It contains allegations of a toxic internal culture, including sexual harassment and gender-based discriminatory practices. Continue reading...

articles.author: Louis Staples
articles.content: The so-bad-it’s-good holiday film has become a new festive tradition. Stars Maddie Ziegler and Dennis Quaid explain why they’re so hard to resist “With the state of the world right now, people want an escape,” says Maddie Ziegler. The 24-year-old performer first shot to fame on the Lifetime reality show Dance Moms in 2011, before becoming the unlikely muse of the publicity-shy singer Sia , which led to a role in Steven Spielberg ’s West Side Story. Ziegler’s latest project is In a Holidaze , a fuzzy Christmas movie that comes to Netflix on 2 December. “I’ve actually never done a romcom before,” she says, speaking on a recent Zoom call from Los Angeles. “I grew up loving Christmas movies so much, so when this came into my lap, I was so excited.’” In the film, Ziegler plays Maelyn – a restless twentysomething who finds herself trapped in a holiday time-loop, where she’s forced to relive the same Christmas at her family’s picturesque cabin until she learns to trust her gut and take chances on what makes her happy. This sugary-sweet movie might be new territory for Ziegler, but it’s exactly the type of film we’ve come to expect from Netflix. The streamer’s Christmas originals usually revolve around romance and family, with an aesthetic quality and winking irony that feels similar to Hallmark – the American card-maker turned movie giant, whose very name is synonymous with cliches. Continue reading...

articles.author: Flora Willson
articles.content: Queen Elizabeth Hall, London George Benjamin and Martin Crimp’s opera was given a skeletal staging where every detail spoke volumes, leaving the LPO to shine in the spotlight It is always a shock to realise how little apparatus theatre really needs. Dan Ayling’s semi-staging of George Benjamin and Martin Crimp ’s 2018 opera played out across a shallow strip in front of the London Philharmonic Orchestra, with singers occasionally slipping between conductor Edward Gardner and the front desks of the strings. Props were minimal but significant: a skipping rope, a glass tumbler, a pot containing a child’s ashes, a crown spotlit on a velvet cushion. There was no set, just five chairs on one side of the podium and one on the other: a succinct image of isolation, of power dynamics skewed. The protagonists of this grim drama about Edward II – the King, his lover, Gaveston, his wife, Isabel, her ally Mortimer – wore sleek black tie except utilitarian, ambitious, underdressed Mortimer. As the Boy was manoeuvred into position as Young King, tenor James Way not only stood taller and held himself more pugnaciously but also put on a tie: every detail spoke volumes. Continue reading...

articles.content: Ava DuVernay’s hugely impressive and unbelievably timely new documentary, and Adrien Brody’s Oscar-wining epic. Plus: Christmas has come early thanks to Arnie! Ava DuVernay, the first Black woman to direct a Best Picture Oscar nominee with 2014’s Selma, is a history-making filmmaker in many ways. A decade after her film 13th was also Oscar-nominated, she’s back with another, even more compelling documentary about democracy under threat. articles.content: (Phantasy Sound) One of the buzziest acts of the 2010s return with One Trip, which bathes their classic sound in a warmer light – until the buzzsaw synths and scattershot percussion explode Devotees still speak in hushed awe about the intense, hypnotic performances by Factory Floor, one of the buzziest electronic groups of the 2010s. Even the band agree: Nik Colk Void (vocalist and modular synth wrangler) wistfully remembered them as “full of carnage” during their lengthy hiatus. So what on earth went down at Mutek Montreal in 2024? Their one-off reunion show proved so transformative that it inspired Factory Floor’s first album in 10 years. Sounding uncharacteristically relaxed, opening single Continuation is a woozier take on their often grinding approach to repetition, building into blissful contentment rather than rabid euphoria. “It’s gonna be fun,” Void exhales. “It’s gonna be … easy.” This third album takes in Factory Floor’s favoured influences – brain-spinning industrial noise, eccentric acid techno, a Kraftwerkian clarity of purpose – and bathes them in a warmer light. But that’s not to say they’ve softened. Standout track Buzz Saw has the album’s toughest synth line, serrated and stomping, for what should be a new live classic. Continue reading...

articles.content: Published nearly two years after his death, this edited selection of the Argentinian pope’s diary capture the profundity of his faith – just don’t expect revelations or raciness When the cardinals in Rome elected the Argentinian Jorge Mario Bergoglio as the 266th pope of the Roman Catholic church in March 2013 – the first Latin American, the first pontiff born outside Europe since the 8th century, the first Jesuit and the first to take the name Francis (after Saint Francis of Assisi) – many of us lapsed Catholics gave a small cheer. Here was a man who looked fair to change the increasingly fusty and conservative, authoritarian and admonitory, tendencies of his two predecessors. Bergoglio seemingly did not want the ceremonial trappings of the office – he’d bought himself a return ticket home to Buenos Aires and caught the bus back to the Vatican guest house where the other cardinals were staying, insisting he would not be moving into the papal apartments overlooking St Peter’s Square. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jude Rogers
articles.content: (Last Night from Glasgow) Russo’s latest album Pe Unde Trece Dorul, roughly translated as Where Longing Goes, is full of surprises – and shows what a fantastically versatile singer she is Long based in Scotland, Lizabett Russo returns to her native Romania for her fifth album of idiosyncratic, spectral folk. Having defied her parents’ wishes to leave the country age 18 and commence her musical journey, she travelled through Transylvania’s remote villages to learn doine (songs) and strigături (traditional rhymed shouts/calls), and named her album after a song taught to her by farmer Maria Dulău, a woman awarded a title to aim for by the Romanian National Institute of Heritage: Living Human Treasure. “Dorul” is like the Welsh hiraeth or Galician saudade , referencing longing and homesickness, and “trece” explains how these feelings travel, wander and pass. Released by the label that also put out Dick Gaughan ’s startling R/Evolution box set, Russo’s album begins like an update of Fourth World music created by trumpeter Jon Hassell and Brian Eno. A sly two-note guitar riff, Tim Lane’s soft drums, and Călin Han’s slowly blown kaval flutter coolness into the air, then Russo joins, multi-tracked and layered in harmony. Her voice is fantastically versatile: gentle yet agile on Bujori (Peonies), sprightly and knowing on Frumoasă-i Nevasta Ta Măi Ghită (Your Wife Is Beautiful, Ghită), It’s also chillingly eerie on Cine Aude Gura Mea (Whoever Hears My Mouth), an a cappella that glistens in shivering reverb. Continue reading...

articles.author: Sylvia Patterson
articles.content: They weathered excess, illness and being dropped and defrauded, but Echobelly are happily back as a duo. Ahead of a new album, they recall the weird fans and cliquey bands of the 90s In 1994, Oasis toured the US for the first time, and a legend quickly emerged: these were Britain’s latest rock’n’roll renegades, who went berserk on crystal meth before a Los Angeles gig and almost split up afterwards. But Sonya Madan remembers it differently. Her band Echobelly were also touring the US that year, and the two groups hung out backstage at each other’s gigs. “I’m gonna blow a myth!” she hoots. “For me, half the stuff about Oasis was made up by their press people. The people around them were partying; everyone was, including us, but it wasn’t that much. Liam was such a sweetheart, I used to go drinking with Noel, we were all mates.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Simon Jenkins
articles.content: The last shake-up, in the 1960s, was based on pure anti-technological snobbery. Let’s put vocational learning back in the heart of our cities What is it about the EU student fees debate that means it has almost derailed Andy Burnham’s Brexit reset? Can the issue be that important? The answer is simple – and, I am sure, personal. Before Brexit, the EU’s citizens, among them its diplomats, were paying the same as UK citizens to have their children’s English perfected at a UK university. Now, some pay up to three times that figure . To put it mildly, they have an interest in persuading the UK government to slash fees. As of now, the issue is still deadlocked. The total cost of meeting the EU’s demand and reducing EU student fees to the new British rate of £9,790 a year has been put at an astronomical £570m a year for Russell group universities alone. Burnham has declined to answer the question of who would foot the bill. Indeed, it is difficult to understand why British taxpayers should subsidise the education of wealthy Europeans. But the cost would then fall on individual universities. The University of St Andrews estimates it would lose a devastating £12m annually. Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.content: Figures indicate England’s players have far more rugby miles in their legs than Saturday’s opponents but Borthwick has managed to balance heavy schedule The prevailing narrative emerging before England’s rematch with New Zealand on Saturday is that the All Blacks are running on fumes. The forwards coach, Jason Ryan, has said that “there is not much juice in the tank” while Graham Henry, who led them to the 2011 World Cup title, has continued the theme in even starker terms. “It’s the end of the season and we’re buggered. They’ve just got no gas in the tank.” It is understood that narrative has raised a number of eyebrows within the England camp. The view, as England seek to clinch a third straight win over New Zealand for the first time in the history of the fixture, is best summed up as, “welcome to our world”. We are nearing the end of a gruelling year for the All Blacks, who give the impression they cannot wait for their season to end, but the grind in England, that which led to Maro Itoje being ordered to take the summer off, is at the very least comparable. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jacob Steinberg
articles.content: The constant turnover of players and staff has made consistency an elusive quality at Stamford Bridge Liam Delap came and went. He joined Chelsea in the summer of 2025 and was hailed by Enzo Maresca as the next Harry Kane. Fast forward a year, though, and there was no chance of Delap joining Kane in England’s World Cup squad. The striker’s form was miserable and the only surprise was that Chelsea made a profit when they sold him to Nottingham Forest for £50m last summer. On one level it looks like good business. Delap’s only season at Stamford Bridge featured one serious hamstring injury, one league goal, one ridiculous red card and not much else. Analysts at other clubs rated him at Ipswich and felt Chelsea was the wrong fit for his direct style of play. The mistake was less the decision not to give Delap another season, no matter the worries over cover for João Pedro, more the call to sign him in the first place. Continue reading...

articles.author: Kathryn Hughes
articles.content: A lexicographer reveals the surprising origins of common zoological turns of phrase, from fat cats to fur babies Anyone who has grown up in the country knows that cows come home. They do it at tea time, like clockwork, because an unmilked cow is an uncomfortable cow. So how did “till the cows come home” come to mean never? Stranger still, when the phrase first appears in a 1587 commentary on St Paul’s epistle to the Galatians, there is only one cow. By the time playwrights Beaumont and Fletcher take it up a few decades later, their characters are kissing and drinking till the cow – still single – comes home. What began as a promise of endless pleasure has become a sigh of futility. Jeremy Butterfield’s Metaphor Zoo is full of such linguistic metamorphoses. Butterfield is a lexicographer by trade, the man the OUP entrusted with revising Fowler’s Modern English Usage. His guiding text is Lakoff and Johnson’s Metaphors We Live By (1980), which argues that metaphors don’t just colour how we speak but structure our thinking. In this sprightly but well-grounded book (metaphor alert), Butterfield asks what mental patterns lie behind the hundreds of animal phrases in English. Then in Johnsonian fashion, he sets about tracing the original, dating each through the Oxford English Dictionary and watching as it goes walkabout. Continue reading...

In this sprightly but well-grounded book (metaphor alert), Butterfield asks what mental patterns lie behind the hundreds of animal phrases in English. Then in Johnsonian fashion, he sets about tracing the original, dating each through the Oxford English Dictionary and watching as it goes walkabout. Continue reading...

articles.author: Andy Beckett
articles.content: ‘Andy time’ may frustrate the media and voters impatient for change – but after years of short premierships and rushed policies, isn’t this the reset Westminster needs? Andy Burnham is making a lot of people impatient. Political journalists, pro-EU activists, climate campaigners, fossil-fuel lobbyists, recipients of welfare benefits, advocates of welfare cuts, enemies of neoliberalism, enthusiasts for renationalisation, members of the armed forces and even cabinet colleagues: all are waiting for the prime minister to make big decisions, and thus reveal the true nature of his administration, four months after its beginning. Since his Manchester mayoralty, some of Burnham’s co-workers have had a phrase for his tendency to take things at his own tempo: “Andy time”. He lets interesting conversations overrun, likes to ponder issues without being rushed, and pushes back crucial announcements. The unveiling of his 10-year plan – a typically ambitious but loose Burnham timespan, and one of his government’s pivotal moments – has been repeatedly delayed. According to the website Politico, it has been pencilled in for 17 December, the final day of the parliamentary calendar. Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.author: Amy-Jane Beer
articles.content: Berwickshire: Between the grey and the red formations, a staggering 65 million years passed. And the Scottish man who figured this out put science into a spin “Who wants to see some reeeally important rocks?” The question sorts my holiday companions into two distinct types, and the self-selecting nerds set out on a blustery clifftop walk. To the north-east, the 320m-year-old volcanic doorstop of Bass Rock contrasts with the edgy artifice of Torness nuclear power station, gleaming in low sun like a radioactive Lego brick. We’re going in search of an even more consequential contrast, but one that is a little harder to see. A series of interpretation stations on the path to Siccar Point encourages us to notice two distinct rock types, old red sandstone and greywacke , and to understand that each was formed in different ways at different times. The greywacke originated in a Silurian ocean 435m years ago, the sandstone in hot deserts of the late Devonian period, 370m years ago. It’s also important to understand that, given enough time, rock can be lifted, rotated, folded and weathered away. That’s what happened to the greywacke, long before the sandstone was laid down on top. Continue reading...

articles.author: Xan Brooks
articles.content: The acclaimed director has announced his latest film Tender Loving Care will be his last. He talks about coming to terms with a life-changing condition and how he would have loved to have made a big budget modern-day movie Mike Leigh and his partner, the actor Marion Bailey, were knocking around at home last Christmas, looking for a good film to watch and constantly coming up short. Finally, Leigh had a brilliant idea. Why not put on Topsy-Turvy, his 1999 costume romp about the making of The Mikado? Problem solved, perfect choice. “It’s not like a habit,” he says hurriedly. “I don’t sit there watching my films every night like Gloria Swanson in Sunset Boulevard. It’s just that Topsy-Turvy happens to be a very enjoyable watch.” The way Leigh sees it, his films are like children. They’ve outgrown him, moved on, but it’s nice to check the family ties are still strong. Some are sunny (Life is Sweet; Happy-Go-Lucky) and some are dour (Naked; Hard Truths), but they all share the same DNA, the same real-world interests and tragicomic mindset. He can’t choose between them; he’ll defend each one to the death. Then he pauses and says, “But I’ve got a soft spot for Meantime.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Eoghan Gilmartin
articles.content: Santiago Abascal’s party has adopted radical ideas from France and beyond. If it joins a PP coalition, it would be a morale boost for allies across the continent It was a scene few would have imagined possible in Spanish politics until recently. Flanked on stage by Catalan flags, the far-right Vox leader, Santiago Abascal, addressed a packed campaign rally in Girona, where he promised “to defend Catalan identity” against supposed “Islamisation”. He urged his audience to confront what he claimed was “the primary challenge” of a new “caliphate” across Spain. For a fringe party that made its breakthrough in 2018 by demonising Catalonia’s independence movement, it was a striking change of emphasis, reflecting a strategic shift that has brought Vox to the brink of power. When the results of this Sunday’s snap general election become clear, there is a strong likelihood that centre-left PM Pedro Sánchez will be forced out, with Vox as kingmakers and junior coalition partners to the traditionally dominant rightwing People’s party (PP). The perpetually dour Abascal may lack the charisma of Trump or Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, but Vox is projected to increase its vote share from 12.4% in 2023 to close to 20% . It has achieved this surge not by moderating its rhetoric as it draws closer to power, but by embracing some of the most radical positions on immigration from across the European far right. A place in government for the party could, in turn, embolden its allies across Europe, as France, Italy and Poland prepare to go to the polls next year. Continue reading...

articles.author: Lucy Mangan
articles.content: The comedian knows how to make perfectly relaxing TV – even as he tries heart-racing new experiences with celebrity pals. From flying a plane loop-the-loop with Mel Giedroyc to bungee jumping with Joanne McNally, it is bliss Alan Carr’s Great Big Bucket List, in which burgeoning national treasure since last year’s win on The Celebrity Traitors Alan tries out an array of experiences accompanied by celebrity pals, is filler TV of the most obvious kind. But this particular varietal has a twist. In this show in which the presenter tries out an array of experiences accompanied by celebrity pals, the presenter feels under no pressure to complete any of the tasks he doesn’t fancy. This makes the Great Big Bucket List the programme of my dreams and Alan my soulmate, my spirit animal, my safe space. Who wants to see people suffering? Pushed beyond their comfort zones? Not me. Why is the world so obsessed with making people uncomfortable? Comfort is the aim . Comfort is great . Comfort is everything . Continue reading...

articles.author: Brian Logan
articles.content: Soho theatre, London The standup throws himself into ‘13 or 14 pieces of humour’ that confirm his gifts for escalating everyday apercus into absurd delights Paul Foot made quite the impression with 2023’s Dissolve , a mid-career breakout from his oddball groove. The Future confirms the 52-year-old as a comic any audience could enjoy, and – to some degree – develops his newfound interest in the real world and the circumstances of his own life. Not that it begins with any seriousness of purpose, as our host throws himself into a series of escalating set pieces built on everyday apercus – how reassuring we find it, say, when a Chinese restaurant is frequented by Chinese diners. Then comes the swerve, which is less well integrated, and less remarkable, than in the show’s predecessor, but affecting nonetheless. Before that, the first half is all about Foot’s free-standing bits (“about 13 or 14 pieces of humour”, he calls them): concentrated bursts of observational comedy, in which he inflates a workaday premise to absurdity and beyond. The etiquette of British funerals; over-excitement at food served on sizzling hot-plates – Foot constructing teetering towers of nonsense from it all with a voice and range of facial expression evoking British comedy at its ooh-missus, nudge-nudge heyday. articles.content: Women suffer the consequences when Catholic healthcare providers acquire hospitals and create geographic deserts for abortion, contraception and IVF In 2012 in Ireland, Dr Savita Halappanavar, who was then 17 weeks pregnant, attended a hospital with back pain. An examination found the pregnancy sac protruding through her womb. Her medical team refused to perform a procedure to end her pregnancy, because in Ireland the law prohibited abortion if a fetal heartbeat was still present. The 31-year-old developed sepsis and subsequently died of a cardiac arrest. During an inquest into her death, a midwife admitted to have said , “We don’t do that [abortion] here. Ireland is a Catholic country.” Halappanavar’s death became a catalyst for the campaign that ultimately led to the legalisation of abortion in Ireland. This would never happen in Australia in 2026, I hear you say. Except, in Australia, Catholic hospitals provide healthcare based on the same Catholic beliefs as Irish hospitals did in 2012. And this scenario could very easily occur in Australia. In 2022, an ABC journalist interviewed an obstetrician working in an Australian Catholic hospital who described admitting a woman at 17 or 18 weeks whose waters had broken and a fetal heartbeat was still present. As the woman’s condition steadily deteriorated, the doctor was unable to recommend the care she required. Continue reading...

articles.content: Liam Delap can exploit Chelsea’s defensive woes while Senne Lammens is under pressure against Brentford Nottingham Forest’s last couple of seasons have been a story of good runs and bad runs, but it may help to know that last season’s encounters with Chelsea both presaged changes of fortune. After they lost to Chelsea in October, a seventh defeat in 10 winless games, Forest’s form improved and they won seven of their next 12 in all competitions. But after beating Chelsea in May, their seventh victory in a 10-game unbeaten run, Forest’s form dipped dramatically and they have won only twice since. Oliver Glasner’s criticism of players whose “standards [are] not high enough” is clearly designed to raise them. Time will tell if it has worked but the key man this week is one who should have no issues with motivation and whose English is at least decent. Liam Delap, facing the side that signed and swiftly discarded him, could really trouble Wesley Fofana and Levi Colwill. The Chelsea centre-back pairing were described as playing like “two novices” by Jamie Carragher after they were outfought by Dominic Calvert-Lewin last week. “Until they sign that dominant centre-back and leader, they’ve got absolutely no chance of achieving anything,” Carragher concluded. Simon Burnton Continue reading...

articles.content: Football seasons can pivot on certain moments and Thomas Frank will hope that Crystal Palace’s turning point came 17 minutes from full time here. Deservedly trailing to Mamadou Sarr’s goal having been second best throughout against Real Sociedad, this game – and perhaps the south London club’s entire trajectory – was turned on its head after Jon Martín was sent off for denying Jean-Philippe Mateta an equaliser. The France striker made no mistake with his penalty before Dwight McNeil – who made up for scoring an own goal in Saturday’s defeat by Coventry capped an extraordinary comeback in Frank’s first home match since succeeding Pierre Sage. Despite Yéremy Pino’s saved penalty in stoppage time and a number of other chances that were squandered, Dean Henderson pulled off a stunning late save to seal the victory and revive Palace’s Europa League campaign. Suddenly Palace have hope where there appeared to be none and the Premier League’s bottom side will head into Sunday’s crucial showdown with Hull with a spring in their step. Continue reading...

articles.content: Ella Purnell is back as a meek but murderous journalist who bumps off bad men. But this isn’t a powerful feminist-revenge tale and it certainly isn’t funny – thankfully, the story is just about saved when a copycat killer arrives Rhiannon Lewis (Ella Purnell) has a nosebleed. It keeps embarrassing her at work and interrupting her when she’s trying to go against her timid nature and assert herself in the office: in nervous or stressful times, pop goes her right nostril. If that weren’t enough of a distraction, at home she has her boyfriend’s corpse stashed in the freezer, concealed beneath an unusual quantity of petits pois. We’re back for a second season of Sweetpea, the crimson-flecked comedy drama where the macabre meets the mundane. In 2024’s first season, local newspaper receptionist Rhiannon was a downtrodden wallflower, if that’s possible, who never got over a childhood during which her mother abandoned the family and her schooldays were ruined by bullying. Having been driven to psychopathy by a thousand microaggressions perpetrated by heedless, selfish men, she found her groove by murdering two boorish strangers before kidnapping her old school bully Julia (Nicôle Lecky) with the intent of killing her. When she discovered Julia’s boyfriend was abusive, Rhiannon offed him instead and allied with Julia. Between them they deflected the attentions of inquisitive junior detective Marina (Leah Harvey), who correctly guessed the identity of the serial killer but was, like her nemesis Rhiannon, a young woman to whom nobody ever listens. Continue reading...

articles.content: Third straight draw leaves title match at 1½–1½ Sindarov drops to eight seconds on move 39 Gukesh Dommaraju plays white after first rest day All your Gukesh v Sindarov questions, answered After two quieter draws, the world chess championship came to life on Thursday as Uzbekistan’s Javokhir Sindarov came within eight seconds of sudden death before fighting back to split the point with India’s Gukesh Dommaraju after nearly five hours. Their spirited 60-move battle at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in the Geneva suburbs left their $2.5m match level at 1½–1½ heading into the first rest day. Gukesh, playing with the black pieces, returned to the Berlin defense of the Ruy Lopez, the opening he used in Tuesday’s 38-move opener . The defending champion sprang the first surprise on move five (5 … Be7), bringing out his bishop before retreating the knight that had taken Sindarov’s e-pawn, putting the challenger behind on time for the first time in the match. After 15 moves, Gukesh still had nearly 1hr 58min of his starting two hours, almost 40 minutes more than his opponent. Continue reading...

articles.content: Before the release of a new documentary, the unrepentant Manchester United icon reflects on his deep bond with English football and his darker instincts “I’m an angel and a demon,” Éric Cantona says intently during a gripping new documentary about his life on and off the football pitch. “And an angel or a demon, you love him or you hate him. I’m far from being the person with the greatest integrity. I’m far from being the person who always tells the truth. I’m far from being the person who has never been hypocritical. Maybe I’m a good person, but I can also be a flower of evil. It’s the first time in my life I’ve realised this. I am a flower of evil, and I find it very beautiful.” It’s hard to know what to expect from the only written interview pinned to the release of Cantona: Flower of Evil . Joel Cantona has warned that his famous brother will walk out at any mention of the enduring crisis surrounding Manchester United , whether it’s a question about Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival or the Glazer family’s ruinous ownership of the club. Continue reading...

articles.content: We put 11 range extenders and mesh systems to the test to find the fastest and most reliable for streaming, gaming and working from home • The best office chairs Fast fibre broadband is fantastic – if the wifi signal reaches the part of your home where you need it. Most of us use the router provided by our broadband provider, often tucked away in a hallway or corner of the lounge. Sadly, these often don’t have the range to cover every room in your home, leaving you high and dry when you’re trying to binge-watch TV or get work done in a distant home office. Wifi extenders and mesh systems can help. Extenders plug in to a mains socket between your location and the router, then pass data backwards and forwards to extend your router’s reach. Mesh systems are even smarter, pairing a secondary router with one or two satellite units, which work together to extend the wifi coverage throughout your home. The mesh system can pass your connection from unit to unit to make sure you’re always getting the best possible link from your device to the internet, wherever you are in your home. Continue reading...

articles.content: Notebooks, clothes and ritual objects taken by British forces in India in the 1930s go on show at Pitt Rivers Museum In 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl called Gaidinliu for leading an uprising against colonial rule. articles.content: Researchers say effects particularly felt in South America where levels plunged even as some areas had extreme rain Extreme global heat caused an unprecedented decline in the water levels of lakes, rivers and reservoirs around the world in 2023 and 2024, an international study has found. The analysis of global water systems, a collaboration led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, found that the planet’s surface freshwater fell sharply during the two years, which were the hottest on record. Global river flows fell to about 5.7% below normal, while the water stored in lakes and reservoirs dropped by 9.5%. Together, this was the largest synchronised decline in surface water since at least 1991. Continue reading...

articles.content: New data offers shocking details of military fatalities. But without domestic accountability, only external pressure can end this conflict The toll of Russia’s war on Ukraine is appallingly evident in the devastation of apartment blocks and hospitals, in the suffering of survivors and, above all, in the mourning of the dead, which included an estimated 150,000 soldiers and at least 18,000 civilians. The toll on Russia’s population has been carefully obscured by Moscow. But a fuller picture has emerged from its own statistics after the hacking group Cyber Partisans, linked to the Belarusian opposition, and the Ukrainian hacker collective Silent Crow obtained 11m death certificates. Analysis by the Guardian offers disturbing insights into the deaths of almost half a million Russians in Ukraine since Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022. articles.content: Ministers have recognised that young adults need more support. But children’s social care reform must go deeper The first lifelong guardianship ceremonies , held in Northampton last week with Josh MacAlister, the children’s minister, among the guests, are the latest in a series of measures aimed at boosting support for care leavers. While the decision to register a link between a person who has been looked after as a child and another adult such as a former carer or friend does not carry legal obligations, those involved spoke movingly about what it meant for these relationships to be formally recognised. New rules requiring councils to support contact between siblings in the care system are similarly aimed at strengthening networks that could sustain them beyond childhood into adult life. Belatedly, the government is acting on a mound of evidence that children who are taken into local authority care are frequently acutely vulnerable when they come out of it as 18-year-olds. Care leavers are over-represented in prisons and homeless shelters, and among those who are not in education, employment or training. In August, the Department for Education published an analysis of 112 deaths of care leavers aged between 18 and 24 in 2025, which made for devastating reading. articles.content: Two former Treasury officials say the value of competition and disruption has become ‘the blind spot of UK economic policy’ The defenestration of Marcus Bokkerink in the Keir Starmer-Rachel Reeves era is half-forgotten now – but the saga was a big deal in January 2025 and should still matter to those at the top of today’s government. Bokkerink was chair of the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) until he was turfed out because, it seemed, he was deemed insufficiently aligned with the Starmer-Reeves idea that regulators should “support growth”. Bokkerink hit back by warning of the dangers of political interference and competition authorities becoming “vulnerable to short-term expediency or vested interests”. Continue reading...

articles.author: Guardian Staff
articles.content: Stephen Childs responds to a letter that said the US software firm was not the right fit for Britain’s health service Prof Caroline Mitchell is right that US systems designed for an insurance market are rife in the NHS ( Letters, 18 November ). But Palantir’s software isn’t among them – and should not be confused with a range of other systems, some designed as far back as the 1970s for billing and then exported to the NHS over the following decades. Our story is different. Each application built on the federated data platform – which connects information across the NHS – is bespoke to the NHS and to the healthcare trust that uses it. The NHS is a highly complex, loose association of healthcare trusts and commissioners, with data that is rich, but often unstructured and frustratingly disconnected. Continue reading...

articles.author: Julie Ward
articles.content: My friend Alison Walton-Robson, who has died aged 61 of ovarian cancer, was a tireless campaigner for the disability arts movement. Latterly she was the creative director of Headway Arts in Blyth, Northumberland, a pioneering inclusive organisation she co-founded in 1995. Headway offers people from all backgrounds the chance to contribute to the cultural life of their communities and to realise their full creative potential. The company, which became an Arts Council England national portfolio organisation in 2023, pays particular attention to providing opportunities for artists who are neurodivergent or have a learning disability, and has built an impressive portfolio of projects, including international collaborations. Allie was proud to be an Erasmus+ ambassador and contributed a case study to the European Movement’s successful campaign for the UK to rejoin the EU Erasmus+ education and training programme. Continue reading...

articles.content: High streets and ultimately the taxpayer will suffer from the chain’s liquidation. Who will benefit? The company that snapped up this institution for just £1 When the bad news came through on his mobile on Wednesday afternoon, the manager of Poundland’s store in Camden, north London, Aboud, summoned all his staff. “One lad, been here 11 years, was in tears and ran out of the store, he was so upset. This is home and family for many of them.” They are among 11,000 staff whose jobs are now at risk, but some shops might get bought by other chains. “Do you know,” Aboud asks me, “can we find out if this store might be saved?” I can’t, and the liquidators are only just starting work. He can no longer get through to his senior regional manager: “He doesn’t pick up now.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Mark Fisher
articles.content: King’s theatre, Glasgow The offensive stereotypes have been ditched but this glitzy panto starring Elaine C Smith shoehorns in plenty of irrelevant material Staging a traditional Aladdin in 2026 is problematic. All those laundry scenes, acrobatics and faux Chinese names have the unpleasant whiff of orientalism. In that sense, it is good to see this glitzy mainstream panto, scripted by Alan McHugh for Crossroads, ditching all that. If only it had not thrown the genie out with the bath water. articles.content: Brighton Dome Boasting all their surviving members, the quartet put on an extraordinarily eclectic and entertaining show, held together by pure ferocity Few punk bands looked destined to make old bones – longevity wasn’t really the point – but you might have got particularly long odds on the Damned lasting any kind of distance. They were “the Bash Street Kids of punk”, in writer Jon Savage’s memorable estimation: “While other groups were carefully considering their moves,” he wrote, “the Damned went out there and pulled faces at the world as if there was no tomorrow.” Even their debut single New Rose implied they knew their time was limited: “I better go,” sang Dave Vanian amid its frantic thunder, “or it’ll be too late.” How wrong can you be? Their peers are long gone or too riven by bad blood to work together, but the Damned are the one major punk band to observe the movement’s 50th anniversary with every surviving original member onstage, something you get the impression even the Damned are faintly startled by. “This is the kind of venue that would have told us to fuck off 50 years ago,” muses guitarist Captain Sensible, as he gazes around the Dome’s stately auditorium. Impressively, a substantial chunk of the audience respond by shouting “fuck off” in unison. Continue reading...

articles.content: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Bayern Munich’s 2-1 defeat to Lille was arguably the most eye-catching of Wednesday night’s Bigger Cup results, but anyone who tuned into proceedings at Stade Pierre-Mauroy will have been unsurprised by the outcome. Not so much an elite European tie as a game of Name That Bayern Reserve, the German champions’ starting lineup resembled a pale facsimile of its usual self. Their current knack-list includes such high-profile names as – deep breath – Harry Kane, Michael Olise, Alphonso Davies, Manuel Neuer, Serge Gnabry, Luis Díaz, Jamal Musiala and Ismael Saibari. And with Díaz and Musiala only fit enough for places on the bench, Konrad Laimer was deployed as a makeshift striker. The veteran right-back is famously as handy as a small pot, but filling Kane’s iconic Skechers proved a task too far for the Austrian. I liked Erling Haaland’s observation that football can simultaneously be “easy and difficult” [yesterday’s Football Daily]. That got me thinking about other things that have conflicting characteristics. Soup can be both sweet and sour. My feelings for my partner often run hot and cold. And my daily tea-timely newsletter can be mildly funny and mildly unfunny – Mike Wilner. The constant change in Watford manager, a once fine club whose first two managers lasted a total of 23 years, is now so high that I don’t even notice it anymore ... apparently this was yesterday, and I’ve no idea who the previous bloke was. Watford are now onto their 30th manager, including caretakers, although in practice they’re all just caretaker managers, since the Pozzos took over in 2012. I don’t know whether to laugh at, or cry for, the Watford fans (Narrator: it’s the former, obviously) – Noble Francis. This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily. To get the full version, just visit this page and follow the instructions . Continue reading...

articles.content: Manchester Collective, Lakeside Arts, Nottingham This take on Luke Mombrea’s Novello-winning work about a fire that burned for two months in Santa Fe, had little need of its billowing video backdrop Premieres are all well and good, but what about second performances, and third and fourth? We puzzle over the problem of new music, of how to build a living classical repertoire, while too often giving new works just one outing to make their case, audiences just one chance to hear them. How brilliant, then, to see American composer Luke Mombrea’s Black Gold – winner of a 2025 Ivor Novello award – at the centre of the Manchester Collective’s new tour: another chance to get our ears around this widescreen soundscape with its slippery electro-acoustic vistas. The fire that raged through the Santa Fe oil fields in 1928 burned for two months, swallowing up the surrounding desert in smoke and ash. Steel plate photographs show derricks dwarfed by pillars of flame and black billowing clouds. They’re the starting point for Mombrea’s chamber work, whose three movements for flute, cello, double bass and percussion were conceived in tandem with Nate Mohler’s monochrome, photo-manipulating video projections. Continue reading...

articles.content: The author blends teen memories and biographical details for a very personal tribute to the late singer When Sathnam Sanghera was a child, his older sisters fell under the spell of Wham!, the pop duo behind hits including Last Christmas and Young Guns (Go for It). Their brother soon caught the bug, becoming a diehard Wham! fan and following the career of singer George Michael into adulthood. In Tonight the Music Seems So Loud, Sanghera blends memoir, biography and cultural criticism as he explores the life and work of Michael via themed chapters covering the singer’s sexuality, activism, addictions, his Greek Cypriot heritage and his songwriting prowess. This is no objective trawl through the life of a distant pop star. Immersing himself in Michael’s world, Sanghera rides the same London bus route that he was on when he wrote Careless Whisper at 17 and visits the restaurant that once belonged to his father (Michael worked there briefly, until his dad fired him for mixing up the drinks orders). Continue reading...

articles.author: As told to Magnus Nome
articles.content: As the Norwegian pop trio’s frontman releases his new album Human Grace, he answers your questions on the devastating effects of fame, living in squalor in London, 80s nostalgia – and a certain bandmate’s denim underwear You ’ ve described your new album, Human Grace, as revealing more of yourself than your previous work. Was there anything you found unexpectedly difficult to express through these songs, or anything that surprised you about yourself during the creative process? BarefootJax No. It’s an exploratory process, the activity of making new music. It’s about quieting yourself, being available to hear tiny little differences in vibes, to pick up a seed that will blossom into something – and then it goes from being nothing to becoming a thing, instantaneously. That has never changed for me. With a-ha, there wasn’t much time and peace for songwriting. Being the frontman takes a lot of focus. What has changed is my access to the skilled tools – singing and guitar – due to the Parkinson’s medication side-effects. For this album, we found old recordings of my voice, some from over 10 years back. It hasn’t been devastating for me to get this diagnosis – it has been a blunt and impactful instrument to stop everything I was doing. I had to reassemble myself first, to understand what it is. Losing access to parts of myself I’ve taken for granted all my life, but also a new appreciation for the architecture of ourselves as an organism – it’s so impressive. It’s mind-blowing. Continue reading...

articles.content: Goodwood Art Foundation The Icelandic artist’s enigmatic monuments, melancholic landscape paintings and never-ending love song are witty, moving and ravishingly conceptual Live in the gallery a man in a dark suit and white shoes leans cabaret-style against a piano and sings about his one great love. “Jenny kissed me,” he intones in a voice both melodic and casually conversational. He croons the words of this love song again, and again, and again. Icelandic artist Ragnar Kjartansson’s durational performance (which means it takes a heck of a long time) is beguiling and beautiful. It’s also a brilliant interpretation of a small masterpiece of English Romantic poetry, Jenny Kiss’d Me, by Leigh Hunt : “Jenny kissed me when we met / Jumping from the chair she sat in.” The poet demands that “Time, you thief” write this down so that he can keep this memory of a perfect moment of love. Continue reading...

articles.content: We’re developing the most powerful tech in history – but trust, safeguarding and privacy are being sidelined in favour of huge profit I’m a senior AI leader at one of the world’s biggest tech companies, and the products we put out into the world are increasingly being recklessly rushed, without proper consideration. The tech industry used to take safety and privacy seriously, but lately I have become worried by how rash we have become. In a sector that is obsessed with being first, ethical hesitation is now viewed as a luxury we can’t afford. If you want to properly understand the actions of big tech, you have to look at the industry’s culture. It moves fast and there is a mindset of constant one-upmanship. articles.content: You don’t have to have sex because it’s ‘what’s expected’, advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. But you may want to be explicit about what you do want Read more Leading questions How do I navigate being single when I’m not interested in sex with near strangers? I don’t judge anyone, consenting adults can do whatever they like – but, for me, sex has to come with trust and, frankly, love, or at least the potential of love. I’m recently single after a long and toxic relationship, and I’ve never dated – I got on the dating scene and found that if I don’t try to get in someone’s pants by the third date, no matter how much of a nice time we’re having, they disappear – and in fact I’ve had some women do the old “call yourself a man” at me, in one memorable case, after they specifically said “not tonight” and I said “no problem” (the response was a frustrated “don’t you have needs?!”). I’ve tried to go along with it and do what’s expected but I don’t enjoy it, it just feels a bit wrong, and when I’ve done this it kills the vibe we had, probably because I can’t get into it properly. I’ve always been into the person, not just the body, but it takes time to get to know someone enough to feel comfortable being intimate. So how can I keep a nice relationship going, so that I can develop the trust I need for sex, without them losing interest because I’m not doing (what I assume) everyone else on the dating scene is doing? Continue reading...

articles.content: Laura van der Heijden/Jâms Coleman (Chandos) The piano-cello duo explore the consoling beauty of works by Franck, Fauré and Mel Bonis, with a welcome rediscovery among the highlights This is the third release from the team of cellist Laura van der Heijden and pianist Jâms Coleman . They say it grew from a desire to record “music of consolation and warmth”, and every piece on this all-French programme fits the bill. The most substantial is Franck’s 1886 Sonata, best known in its original, violin-and-piano version but also claimed by cellists ever since the composer sanctioned an arrangement not long after its premiere. It gets a persuasively expansive performance here. Coleman’s piano is unfailingly clear and detailed; van der Heijden’s playing is angry and urgent in the second movement, impassioned in the climactic passages of the finale. More generally, though, her melodies spool out in endless lines, her tone rich and sustained, her phrasing unbroken almost to a fault: just occasionally the cello line feels as if it could use more breath, more space in which to ask questions. There’s a sense of security in that sustained tone, though, and it serves the consolatory aspect of the programme well. Massenet’s Méditation from Thaïs and Fauré’s bittersweet Sicilienne are the most familiar of the shorter pieces; alongside these there are a transcription of Paix, a melancholy yet consolatory song by Charlotte Sohy; the compact and characterful Three Pieces by Nadia Boulanger; and a characteristically lovely Élégie by the still-underrated Darius Milhaud. And from Franck’s protege Mel Bonis we hear the 1904 Cello Sonata, a searching work that manages to feel tautly argued and rhapsodic at the same time – a worthwhile rediscovery. Continue reading...

articles.content: ​I set out to visit the supermarket in Vatican City and discovered who can actually shop there and what they might be cooking A couple of years ago, it was announced that the supermarket inside Vatican City was to be taken over by the Gabrielli group and become one of their medium-sized Tigre stores “known for daily freshness and a welcoming and courteous atmosphere”. I remember reading this announcement in Roma Today and assuming the new supermarket would be like the impeccably efficient Vatican post office and open to everyone, and that one day I would share a freezer aisle with cardinals, nuns and off-duty Swiss Guards. Fast forward two years to the Feast team’s discovery that Vatican City is one of two countries in which there are no Feast app users (the other is North Korea). “What do they eat in Vatican City?” was the next question. Bingo, I thought, knowing exactly where Vatican residents do at least some of their shopping. Here was my chance to shop and to investigate, and to see if the special offers at our local Tigre are the same as in Papa Leo XIV’s hood in Vatican City, the smallest independent state in the world. Continue reading...

articles.content: Having built its reputation on big, brash reds, the centre of US winemaking is keeping pace with changing tastes and now becoming known for crisp whites, too I was always more of a Dawson’s Creek girlie than a fan of The OC , yet the subject of this column has found me wrestling with the earworm that is the latter’s theme tune : “California, here we come/Right back where we started from.” For Scribe Winery , at the southern end of the Sonoma Valley, this is apt, though I’m not sure winemaker Andrew Mariani would thank me for the comparison. Since buying 100 hectares here in 2007, he and his brother, Adam, have been restoring the land to viticulture after an interlude as a turkey farm. Some of the Marianis’ vines are riesling and sylvaner, honouring the German immigrant family who first cultivated them here in the 1850s, but they make up a small proportion of Scribe’s production, which is focused on bright, bracing chardonnay and terroir-driven pinot noir. It’s an approach that reflects the trend of drinkers turning away from the beefy reds, particularly cabernet sauvignon, that made California famous, towards fresher – dare I say Old World? – styles. Andrew has pulled up “cab” on recently acquired land to make room for more pinot, and his chardonnays see no oak, which has long been associated with California whites. Some even go into keg, making them more accessible. Continue reading...

articles.author: Tariq Goddard
articles.content: Bournemouth International Centre Kicking off yet another UK leg of his Never Ending Tour, Dylan may seem to treat his audience with indifference – but his songs are given imaginative, probing arrangements Norman Mailer once asked whether a reader would finish The Old Man and the Sea if they did not already know Ernest Hemingway was the author. There are moments during this Bob Dylan set – the first of another UK leg of his so-called Never Ending Tour – where I wonder what we would make of tonight’s music if we were not aware of the identity of the now 85-year-old performer. Ever since beginning the Never Ending Tour in the late 80s, Dylan has disdained crowd pleasing platitudes, preferring to reinterpret his vast oeuvre in his inimitable “late style”: the subdued jazz version of Tangled Up in Blue dropped halfway through the show is typical of his tendency to insulate old material in a new arrangement. Dylan’s decision to kick off these dates in Bournemouth at a time of year when the town’s wealthy snowbirds will have headed farther south, exhibits the same wilfulness, as does the very way he performs on stage. One can imagine Dylan rattling through tonight’s set even if the BIC were empty, a scenario completely congruous with his apparent indifference to the audience hellbent on deciphering his every syllable. Continue reading...

articles.content: Batter assumes vice-captaincy and is set to step in as skipper in Canberra, with appointment a potential pointer to side’s future limited-overs direction When Will Jacks broke his hand at the MCG last Saturday night – his birthday ruined and his tour of Australia over – there were a few directions England could have turned as regards the vice-captaincy. Plenty of teams happily do without an official deputy, of course. But with Harry Brook jetting off to join the Test tour of South Africa after the fourth of these five T20 internationals, a replacement will be required when the series wraps up in Canberra. Phil Salt was one option. For all of his unfettered aggression, powered by those tattooed, Popeye-like forearms, the opener is an intelligent, thoughtful cricketer very much in tune with the rhythms of T20. As well as two seasons captaining in the Hundred, most recently with Welsh Fire, Salt previously deputised for Jos Buttler against Australia at home two years ago. Continue reading...

articles.content: PC; Cosy Lives/Free Lives Catering to the exacting whims of a small town preparing for some grand visitors presents absorbing, beautifully designed – and surprisingly thrilling – challenges The small town of Twillford is abuzz with intrigue and excitement. A local duke has died and ladies of a certain standing are determined to make an impression at the funeral. As a newly arrived dressmaker with the only clothing shop in the area, you’re about to get plenty of work. Thus begins this utterly delightful sim game, in which you talk to customers, gather their style preferences and tailor specific outfits just for them. It could be a suitably respectful funeral frock, with just a hint of style to catch the eye of the duke’s wealthy relatives, or perhaps a work outfit for a farmer who loves bright colours. Once you have your brief, you open your sketchbook and draft a pattern using fabric swatches and a pencil to colour in your design. Need something elegant? How about a strapless bodice. An outfit for the office? A pencil skirt is a good call. Continue reading...

articles.author: Alexis Petridis
articles.content: ( Mashwrks) Sharp, unsentimental rhymes and a fearless disregard for genre make Scenes a richly varied victory lap for for one of grime’s most distinctive talents It’s not often that a UK rap album arrives accompanied by its own air freshener and video game, but here we are. Head over to Novelist’s website, and you can find not merely the usual means of promoting a new release – branded hoodies, T-shirts and so on – but a scented mirror hanger that bears the album’s artwork and Scenes: the Drive, a vaguely Mario Kart-ish arcade game that involves driving around the landmarks of London and Los Angeles avoiding buses and the attentions of the traffic police to the strains of an album track called Prime. But then, from the moment he appeared on the grime scene in his teens – so young he now constitutes an elder statesman in his late 20s – the south Londoner has cut something of a maverick figure in the world of UK rap. He arrived bearing a moniker that seemed oddly bookish among his more grittily named peers. His early releases saw him working alongside defiantly left-field producer Mumdance. He attracted a lot of press attention of the “grime’s brightest new hope” variety, but seemed to last about 20 minutes on the high-profile XL label before departing to start his own imprint, Mmmyeh. Continue reading...

articles.content: He may be a proud petrolhead with a racing licence … but superstars have been lured in before then flounced off. The BBC simply can’t afford for that to happen again There is a lot riding on 2028’s Top Gear revival. Ever since The Punch That Changed Everything, the series has ostensibly remained the BBC’s landmark motoring show, even though several successive iterations have demonstrably been nothing of the sort. But hope springs eternal, and this time the BBC seems to be pinning everything it’s got on Gordon Ramsay. And, look, let’s get the bad stuff out of the way first. At first glance this looks very much like the BBC has done another Joey. Ramsay is a huge name. Famous, wealthy, instantly recognisable and with global appeal, he has the potential to open Top Gear up to a brand new audience. Continue reading...

articles.author: Frédéric Noy
articles.content: It takes three years for shipbuilders in the 16th-century port of Mandvi to complete a commission, in a trade that is as cultural as it is technical In the 16th century, the port city of Mandvi on India’s west coast was founded by the rulers of the kingdom of Kutch, and quickly established itself as one of the most dynamic ports in the western Indian Ocean. Its strategic geographical position, along the estuary of the Rukmavati River, which flows into the Arabian Sea in the Gulf of Kutch, and mastery of monsoon wind navigation enabled it to become part of vast maritime networks connecting India to the Gulf, the Arabian peninsula and east Africa. Mandvi prospered through trade, exporting cotton textiles, indigo, cereals and handicrafts, while importing dates, pearls, Arabian horses and luxury goods. A stemson, a piece of supporting timber in the bow of a boat, is carved from teak in a Mandvi shipyard under supervision by the master shipwright, or mistri, who designs boats without written plans. All photographs: Frédéric Noy Continue reading...

articles.author: Emine Saner
articles.content: Thirty years after the roles that made her famous, the star of Three Colours: White and the Before trilogy is busier than ever – as a screenwriter and director. But, she says, a lot of people have tried to keep her down To listen to Julie Delpy talk about her workload is to feel the need for a nap coming on. She is writing six screenplays at the moment that range from dark comedies to thrillers. “I don’t do monoculture,” she says. If her producer hadn’t reined her in, she would be working on five horror film scripts too. The actor, writer and director says she doesn’t sleep well – she can sit at her desk for up to 18 hours, writing “until I run out of steam. I know you could think I’m exaggerating. I’m not. If you look at my computer, you will see how bad it is.” We’re on a video call, Delpy from her home in Los Angeles. She is charming – intense and funny in big black-framed glasses. “I look so weird with this angle on my hair,” she says, of the ceiling light behind her. “Like an angry bald man!” Continue reading...

articles.content: The quarterback’s spectacularly messy exit from Pittsburgh could herald an overdue collapse at one of the NFL’s most famous franchises Nobody in the world, except maybe Pittsburgh Steelers owner Art Rooney II, is surprised that the franchise’s marriage of convenience with Aaron Rodgers ended in spectacular flames . Despite their own elevated idea of themselves, Pittsburgh have been one of the NFL’s messiest soap operas for a solid decade. When they linked up with the league’s messiest quarterback, it seemed certain we would get … even more mess. When they doubled down last offseason by hiring the coach with whom Rodgers had fallen out in Green Bay in the late 2010s, the mess became inevitable. We’d seen hints of the approaching drama in the season’s first 11 weeks. “What the fuck … call it!” Rodgers yelled at McCarthy as he looked for a play in early October. Continue reading...

articles.author: Devi Sridhar
articles.content: Protein is the food industry’s current nutritional good guy. The fact that it’s often added to ultra-processed food makes it anything but When I was growing up in the US in the 1980s and 90s, fat in foods was demonised . Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine were all the rage, with the message that fat was bad for our hearts and arteries . By the early 2000s, concern had moved to added sugar and its apparent links to obesity and type 2 diabetes , driving food reformulations. Sugar was replaced with artificial sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame K, which have their own health impacts. Aspartame is classified by the World Health Organization as possibly carcinogenic in humans, while observational research such as a 2022 study of about 102,000 adults has linked acesulfame K with increased cancer risk. Then carbohydrates came into the spotlight, with pasta, rice and bread becoming the bad guys for our diet and blamed for weight gain. There is a fashion cycle in nutrition, where each food group or ingredient takes its turn being blamed for our poor health. Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Continue reading...

articles.author: Kat Lister
articles.content: The co-director of An Eye for an Eye, Tanaz Eshaghian, reveals how she came to make a documentary about a woman facing the threat of execution from her husband’s family – as sanctioned by sharia law “Even though I was raised here,” says the Iranian-American film-maker Tanaz Eshaghian from her home in New York, “I was brought up with the understanding that there are things that you do and things that you don’t do.” Take her 2006 autobiographical feature, Love Iranian-American Style, about her experience of dating in her 20s, which was, she says, “about how I was supposed to marry a nice Iranian man and stay a virgin”. But by the time she’d graduated from Brown University in Rhode Island “that ship had sailed”, she laughs. Since Love Iranian-American Style, she has made equally taboo-breaking documentaries about a women’s prison in Afghanistan (Love Crimes of Kabul, 2011), trans people in Iran (Be Like Others, 2008) and disabled teenagers in Pakistan (As Far As They Can Run, 2022). And with each new project, the duality of her heritage (Eshaghian emigrated to the US not long after the Iranian revolution when she was six) has spurred her to focus eastwards, closer to where she was born. “When you’ve been raised in the west you can see how similar the thinking is,” Eshaghian says of the similarities she’s found there: “the conservative thinking, the place of women, what’s allowed, what’s important”. articles.description: The co-director of An Eye for an Eye, Tanaz Eshaghian, reveals how she came to make a documentary about a woman facing the threat of execution from her husband’s family – as sanctioned by sharia law “Even though I was raised here,” says the Iranian-American film-maker Tanaz Eshaghian from her home in New York, “I was brought up with the understanding that there are things that you do and things that you don’t do.” Take her 2006 autobiographical feature, Love Iranian-American Style, about her experience of dating in her 20s, which was, she says, “about how I was supposed to marry a nice Iranian man and stay a virgin”. But by the time she’d graduated from Brown University in Rhode Island “that ship had sailed”, she laughs. Since Love Iranian-American Style, she has made equally taboo-breaking documentaries about a women’s prison in Afghanistan (Love Crimes of Kabul, 2011), trans people in Iran (Be Like Others, 2008) and disabled teenagers in Pakistan (As Far As They Can Run, 2022). And with each new project, the duality of her heritage (Eshaghian emigrated to the US not long after the Iranian revolution when she was six) has spurred her to focus eastwards, closer to where she was born. “When you’ve been raised in the west you can see how similar the thinking is,” Eshaghian says of the similarities she’s found there: “the conservative thinking, the place of women, what’s allowed, what’s important”. articles.author: Eloise Cooke
articles.content: A new exhibition celebrates landmark artists who sliced up existing works to make striking new pieces. The show’s curators discuss how, in order to create, sometimes you first need to destroy When Valerie Solanas sold her SCUM Manifesto in 1967 it was priced at 10 cents for women and $1 for men. Artist Justine Kurland considered doing something similar with her “man books”: sell them off cheap to undermine their cultural weight. But knowing that people would just flip the books for a profit, instead she took a knife to what she calls the “problem of language and history and inheritance” in photography. She went through her own library of canonical male photographers, cut up the books and made collages from the spoils. Kurland called the project SCUMB (Society for Cutting Up Men’s Books), after Solanas’s manifesto. The same idea underpins What Rose from the Cut, a group show at Graces Mews Gallery in south London. Co-curated by Kurland, the V&A Parasol Foundation curator of women in photography Fiona Rogers, and collector Sarah Miller Meigs, the show brings together more than 40 artists working in collage, photomontage and assemblage, across three generations. All the artists share a simple aim: to make something new out of something already there. The result is no one thing: the show is erotic, sentimental, irreverent and sobering, often all at once. “There is something very specific to the idea of what it is to tear something apart,” Kurland says. “There are so many things that collage immediately does right out the door.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Ed Aarons
articles.content: Crystal Palace’s influential supporters’ group disbanded 24 hours before their first home game this season – and Selhurst Park has not been the same since Simon Teesdale could not help feeling mixed emotions when his beloved Crystal Palace won the Conference League in Leipzig in May. He started going to Selhurst Park with his father in the 1980s, became a season-ticket holder in the 1990s and has watched with pride as the club established itself as a permanent fixture in the Premier League over the past 14 years. Palace finally secured a major trophy in the 2025 FA Cup final – an experience Teesdale remembers as “one of the best days of my life” – and followed that up by winning the Conference League but he decided in August not to renew his season ticket. “Something happened between the FA Cup win and today that changed me,” he wrote in an emotional article published last month on his website. “Tipped me over the edge. Actually, it’s fairer to say that something accelerated in that period of time. The seeds were sown years ago.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Daniel Dylan Wray
articles.content: Backed by the KLF, a monument is being built using 34,592 bricks, each containing a deceased person’s glazed ashes. Is this the future of funerals? We join emotional marchers on Birkenhead’s smoky, noisy Day of the Dead Hundreds of people wearing hi-vis clothing are on a death march through Birkenhead Park. A burning shopping trolley leads the way, smoke grenades clog the air, and people holding traffic signs chant: “The dead don’t stop – till they reach the top.” There’s a wave of curtain-twitching from residents who look on with fear and bemusement as what looks like a psychedelic building site gone rogue marches through their beautiful recreation space. Where could they be going? The answer might shock some of them. For this crowd are on their way to build a pyramid … made of dead people. “My brother calls it my ‘anarchist death cult,’” laughs Steve Lowe, chief engineer of L-13 Light Industrial Workshop, who is involved in running Birkenhead Day of the Dead and the People’s Pyramid. It’s an event that has taken place every year (except 2020) since 2018 in a variety of locations and was announced by Jimmy Cauty and Bill Drummond of the KLF (AKA the Justified Ancients of Mu Mu AKA K2 Plant Hire Ltd), the seminal electronic duo and experimental art provocateurs, when they returned after 23 years in 2017. Continue reading...

articles.author: Chris Wiegand
articles.content: A wave of shows, including High School Musical and Rent, are upping the drama by placing viewers alongside actors. What are the risks and rewards? In the socially distanced summer of 2020, Jesus Christ Superstar was staged at Regent’s Park in London for a hugely pruned audience. Like the actors, we were kept two metres apart. It was a triumphant but extremely strange experience – not least from my current perspective. I’m standing on stage at Theatre Royal Drury Lane, jostling alongside other theatregoers, watching a miraculous revival of the same production. But this time, 75 audience members have been given a spot within the scaffold-style set for the show, beneath the musicians and almost side by side with the cast. We feel the energy of the ensemble’s dance moves, seem to join the crowd of Jesus’s followers – and those who conspire against him – and come extraordinarily close to the musical’s star, Sam Ryder, who rests right by my feet after his solo Gethsemane. It’s as close as I’ve been to the beating heart of a big West End production. Until, that is, the following week when I watch the captivating revival of Rent at the Tom Stoppard theatre from one of 82 audience seats arranged in a semicircle on stage. (Mine is just beneath a shelf bearing candle-filled wine bottles – a marker of La Vie Bohème.) Stranger Things’ Gaten Matarazzo bounds past on to the stage, the actors mingle with us and the band are only just out of reach. Continue reading...

articles.author: Rebecca Wait
articles.content: The beautiful and mercenary Honey is a monstrously compelling character, in a novel with the ruthlessness of Richard Yates but more wit ‘A sweet white grape of a book” is how Virginia Woolf described Elizabeth Jenkins’s first novel, Virginia Water, published in 1929 when Jenkins was 24. Jenkins may have detected a condescending note. She was wary of Woolf, having been invited into the Bloomsbury inner circle and then (in her own view, at least) just as quickly dropped again. Jenkins soon regretted the novel’s publication, apparently afraid acquaintances might recognise themselves, and tried to get rid of as many copies as she could. Fortunately she wasn’t long deterred, either by her uneasy dealings with Woolf or her anxiety about Virginia Water; her subsequent literary career spanned 70 years, though most of her books had fallen out of print by the time she died in 2010. Perhaps this reissue of her 1968 novel, Honey, will bring Jenkins back into fashion. It ought to. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jon Bryant
articles.content: Market stalls are laden with local delicacies in the run-up to Christmas, while the city’s elegant cafes make the perfect spot to sit and watch the world go by Famous for its fabulous fruit and vegetable markets, Aix-en-Provence extends its stalls in winter to include les treize desserts de Noël , the 13 desserts of a traditional Provençal Christmas. I buy almonds (which represent the Carmelites), dried figs (Franciscans), walnuts (Augustinians) and raisins (Dominicans) from the Place Richelme market. Then I queue up in the Place des Prêcheurs for oreillettes (sweet, ear-shaped wafers), gingerbread, and white and black nougat (representing good and evil). Calissons d’Aix, the city’s celebrated, lozenge-shaped sweets, come from the smart Brémond or Le Roy René confiseries nearby. These desserts are laid out on tables in Provençal homes for the Christmas period interspersed with santons (tiny clay figurines), which are sold at Aix’s Foire aux Santons from mid-November. Also displayed alongside the usual Nativity figures in the churches and tourist office, these feature hundreds of Provençal characters including bakers, wet nurses, beekeepers, a pétanque player and the artist Paul Cézanne, who was born in the city, all grimacing to reflect the drudgery of daily life. In January there is even a nativity play, La Pastorale Maurel , at Aix’s Théâtre du Jeu de Paume, with humans playing the still-grimacing santons. Continue reading...

articles.content: Deprivation is behind the sharp rise highlighted in the Natsal study, and that’s an outrage. High energy bills should never be a factor in reproductive choice The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal) is the crowdpleaser of the data world. Nerds love it because of its extraordinary thoroughness. It’s one of the largest studies of sexual behaviour in the world, surveying nearly 7,000 people in the UK between the ages of 16 and 59, once a decade. Everyone else loves it because they get to talk about sex. Some of the statistics speak for themselves – among 25- to 34-year-old women, the number who say they never want children has gone up fourfold, a sad, completely understandable reflection of the outside world. Other figures, though, are mysterious: the number of women aged 16 to 24 who are on the pill has dropped precipitously , from nearly half to less than a third. Over the same period, the online space has been flooded with information about hormonal contraception, some of it better than it has ever been – more accessible, more accurate – and some of it plain wrong. Is there strategic, funded disinformation coming from Christian fundamentalists, such as we have already seen in the abortion space, where anti-abortion activists hose money at putatively “grassroots” online influencers ? Or is it a quirk of the algorithms that once you go down the rabbit hole of “has the pill made me depressed?”, you will be shown endless influencers who have experienced that very (improbable) thing? It’s hard for a young person to navigate what’s real, and it’s hard to distinguish superstition from preference. articles.content: Timms review tackles some big questions about a flawed system – but leaves other issues in the ‘maybe later’ drawer Stephen Timms would be forgiven for feeling his thunder has been stolen. The minister for social security has spent the last year reviewing personal independence payments (Pip) in light of Keir Starmer’s doomed measures last summer, but last week the Milburn review pitched a set of changes to the key disability benefit to great fanfare. But when Timms took to the House of Commons to call for a “fundamental overhaul” of Pip on Tuesday, it was clear these were altogether bigger – and notably not explicitly cost-saving – ideas. articles.author: Rachel Roddy
articles.content: Soft, plump, sweet-savoury rolls marry historical English breakfast baps with a culinary tradition from Italy’s mountainous Trentino-Südtirol In Elizabeth David’s English Bread and Yeast Cookery , there’s a chapter called “Manchets, Mayn and Payndemayn”, all of which were 15th-century names for rarefied soft white bread made from the finest wheat flour. As well as pages of historical context that only she could make so lively, David includes a 1615 recipe for manchet from a book called The English Huswife that calls for meal to be ground into the whitest flower, mixed with ale yeast, salt and liquor (a mixture of water and milk), before being wrapped in a cloth, kneaded with feet, left to swell, shaped, then baked in a gentle heat. It is this form of manchet that David sees as being the common ancestor of all English breakfast breads: baps, soft rolls and dough cakes, with the presence of milk (and, therefore, fat) ensuring both crumb and crust are soft. In fact, her recipe for breakfast baps (or, rather, a recipe from Mr CG Lockyer from Crewkerne) is almost identical to manchet, although without the millstones, dough tub and feet. Continue reading...
